https://aeon.co/essays/instrumentalisati.standfirst: Philosopher Julian Baggini argues that treating art, relationships and even leisure chiefly as instruments for other ends can obscure their intrinsic worth. The essay challenges an exclusively productivity-based account of value.
body: The essay asks whether things must serve a further purpose to be valuable.

Baggini's thesis is that instrumental reasoning can be appropriate but becomes impoverishing when it crowds out intrinsic value: friendship for its own sake, art experienced rather than optimized, and leisure that need not justify itself.

Instrumental value means something is useful as a means; intrinsic value means it is worth having or doing in itself. Both can coexist, but measuring every activity by outputs risks losing the second.
An example: a walk can improve fitness, but treating it only as exercise may erase the pleasure of looking and wandering.

A serious objection is that material scarcity requires tradeoffs, and practical benefits are often part of why an activity is possible. The argument need not deny that; it warns against making utility the only lens.
A possible response is to reserve space for ends that need no external productivity justification, while still recognizing the constraints under which people live.
This connects to Aristotle's distinction between activities pursued for themselves and instrumental tasks, and to modern debates about commodification and attention.
If the argument is right, institutions might measure fewer aspects of life solely by efficiency; individuals might ask whether optimization is helping or replacing an experience.
Open questions: When is a useful side benefit harmless? Can public institutions protect intrinsically valuable activities without imposing a particular ideal of the good?
